title: 'Ramayana' Wants to Throw Its Grand Premiere in Dubai — and the Diaspora Is the Whole Point
excerpt: Ranbir Kapoor's Ram, Sai Pallavi's Sita and Yash's Ravana on one red carpet: the makers of India's most ambitious epic are reportedly scouting Dubai venues with NRIs squarely in mind.
body:
Imagine it: a warm Dubai night, the skyline lit like a circuit board, and a red carpet long enough to land a plane on. **Ranbir Kapoor** steps out as Lord Ram. **Sai Pallavi** beside him as Sita. And then, drawing the loudest roar of the night, **Yash** — the KGF storm himself — arriving as Ravana. That is the spectacle the makers of **Ramayana** are reportedly chasing, and after months of stop-start uncertainty, the plan is back on the table.

<youtube></youtube>

According to a *Mid-Day* report, the team behind India's most ambitious film in years has revived discussions to host a grand premiere in Dubai. The idea had been parked back in April — "the timing didn't feel right," a source said, citing the regional situation — but with conditions easing, location scouts are reportedly already evaluating venues across the city. "The city was always the preferred choice," the source explained, "because of its ability to stage large-scale events and the Indian diaspora." Read that last phrase again. This is a film studio openly admitting that the NRI audience isn't an afterthought to the rollout — it's a reason to fly the whole cast halfway across the Gulf.

> "The city was always the preferred choice because of its ability to stage large-scale events and the Indian diaspora." — Source quoted in Mid-Day

Nothing is confirmed yet. The makers haven't officially signed off on Dubai, and a premiere abroad lives or dies on logistics, security and timing. But the very fact that **Ramayana** is courting the diaspora this aggressively tells you everything about the scale of what's coming.

And the scale is genuinely staggering. Directed by **Nitesh Tiwari** — the man who made *Dangal* — and backed by producer **Namit Malhotra** of Prime Focus Studios, *Ramayana* is being mounted as a two-part, six-hour-plus epic. Part 1 is targeting Diwali 2026, with reports suggesting a possible move to October 30 — a week ahead of the festival — to give it a longer, uninterrupted run. Part 2 follows on Diwali 2027. The cast reads like a national event: Ranbir as Ram (and, he let slip in a recent interview, Lord Parashuram in a dual role), Sai Pallavi as Sita, Yash as Ravana, **Sunny Deol** as Hanuman, **Ravi Dubey** as Lakshman, and — in a goosebump-inducing bridge across generations — **Arun Govil**, the Ram of the beloved 1980s TV series, reportedly stepping in as King Dashrath.

Then there's the sound. The score is being composed jointly by **A.R. Rahman** and **Hans Zimmer** — the man who gave you *Roja* and the man who gave you *Inception*, sharing a single baton. If that pairing doesn't make the hair on your arms stand up, check your pulse. Trade reports peg a theatrical distribution deal in the region of ₹450 crore, which would make it one of the costliest releases India has ever attempted.

Tiwari, for his part, has been careful about the weight he's carrying. In a recent conversation he described himself as a devout follower of the epic and said his own satisfaction is his benchmark for not bruising the audience's faith. He's promised that the VFX-heavy vision of Ayodhya and Lanka is meant to *enhance* the story, not drown it — that the soul of the film lives in "morals, principles, and relationships," not just spectacle. It's a delicate tightrope: make it grand enough to justify the budget, reverent enough not to offend, and human enough to move people who've known this story since childhood.

For the diaspora, *Ramayana* is shaping up to be more than a film — it's a homecoming on a screen. For NRIs raising kids who know more about Marvel than Mahishmati, here is the foundational Indian epic rendered with Hollywood-grade craft and a cast they actually follow on Instagram. A Dubai premiere would put a flag in the ground: a marquee Indian event, staged in a city that is itself half-Indian, beamed out to the world. Expect the usual diaspora rollout to be enormous — IMAX bookings across the US, UK and Canada, multiple dub languages, and the kind of opening-weekend temple-and-theatre energy that only a handful of films generate.

There are reasons for measured expectations. The first teaser drew a slice of online negativity alongside the praise — some quarrelled with Ranbir's look, others with the VFX. Adapting the *Ramayana* in a polarised climate is a minefield; one misjudged frame can ignite a week of outrage. And six hours across two years is a long bet on sustained audience patience. But the ambition is undeniable, and the diaspora-first instinct is the smartest thing about the campaign.

A Dubai premiere isn't locked. But picture it anyway — Ram, Sita and Ravana under the desert lights, an ocean of NRIs in their best clothes, and a story older than memory arriving like it's brand new. If the makers pull it off, it won't just be a premiere. It'll be a statement about who Indian cinema is really making these films for now. Spoiler: it might just be you.
